lead: A data acquisition system (DAS) reads many sensors and turns their voltages into numbers a computer can store, compare and plot. One analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) is shared among many channels, so the designer must fix three things: the smallest voltage step the system can see, how many samples per second each channel gets, and the order in which channels are read. DAS hardware sits inside power-plant monitoring racks, patient monitors, machine-tool controllers, water-treatment panels and student lab benches.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for signal conditioning, and the dynamic characteristics in Unit 1 for response and settling time.

blocks.text: A DAS is a chain. Each block hands a signal to the next, and the weakest block sets the accuracy of the whole reading. The order is fixed, and the figure shows it left to right.

items: Transducer converts the physical variable (temperature, pressure, strain) into an electrical quantity. Its output may be a few millivolts, a resistance change or a current.
Signal conditioner amplifies, filters, linearises and isolates that output, delivering a standard range such as 0-5 V or 4-20 mA. See Chapter 6.1.
Multiplexer is a switch bank that connects one input channel at a time to the shared converter. Eight or sixteen channels to one ADC is common.
Sample-and-hold freezes the selected voltage on a capacitor while the ADC works, so the input does not move during conversion.
ADC converts the held voltage into a binary number. Its bit count sets the resolution and its conversion time sets the speed.
Processor or controller selects channels, starts conversions, scales raw counts into engineering units (degrees Celsius, kPa, newton) and applies limits.
Store and display or bus keeps the numbers locally, shows them on a screen, or sends them over RS-485, Ethernet, USB or a fieldbus to a supervisory system.

blocks.text: The multiplexer is what makes a DAS cheap: one accurate converter serves many sensors. The price is time. Every extra channel scanned is time the converter cannot spend on another channel.

sections.h3: Resolution, sampling rate and channel scan

blocks.text: Resolution is the smallest voltage change the converter can distinguish. It depends only on the full-scale span and the number of bits.

blocks.where: ΔV is the resolution in volts (one least significant bit, 1 LSB); V_FS is the full-scale span in volts, the difference between the highest and lowest input, so a ±5 V range has V_FS = 10 V; n is the ADC bit count and 2ⁿ the number of output codes.

blocks.text: Speed is shared. The converter produces numbers at a fixed total rate, and the multiplexer divides that rate among the scanned channels.

blocks.where: f_ch is the samples per second each channel gets, in samples/s (S/s); f_total is the total converter rate in S/s; N is the number of channels actually scanned; T_conv is the time allowed for one conversion, in seconds, including multiplexer settling and sample-and-hold acquisition.

blocks.text: The sampling rule follows from f_ch. To reconstruct a waveform, the highest frequency present in that channel must stay below half its own sample rate: f_max < f_ch / 2 (the Nyquist limit). A 1 kS/s channel therefore handles signals up to 500 Hz. When the input carries faster components they fold down as false slow waves, which is why the conditioner's low-pass filter is placed before the multiplexer. The full mathematics of aliasing is in Chapter 6.10.

A sample-and-hold circuit closes a switch, charges a capacitor to the input voltage, then opens. The ADC converts the frozen value. Two times matter. The acquisition time is how long the capacitor takes to settle to the new input. The aperture time is the short, uncertain window when the switch opens; a changing input gives an error of (rate of change) × (aperture time). A 1 V/µs ramp with a 50 ns aperture smears the sample by 50 mV, which is 20 LSB for a 12-bit converter on a 10 V span. A sample-and-hold is compulsory whenever a slow converter must read a signal that changes quickly during the conversion time.

items: Successive approximation (SAR): compares the input against a trial word bit by bit; medium speed, medium cost, the usual general-purpose choice.
Flash: 2ⁿ − 1 comparators compare the input against every decision level at once, converting in a single step; fastest, expensive, used for video and radar.
Sigma-delta: oversamples and filters; slow per sample but very high resolution and excellent noise rejection, used for thermocouples and load cells.

blocks.text: Three system architectures carry these blocks into the field. A PC plug-in card puts the multiplexer, ADC and bus interface on one board inside a desktop, cheap for a lab. A stand-alone unit is a boxed instrument with its own display and memory, used where no computer sits. A distributed or SCADA system spreads small remote units near the plant and links them to a central master over a fieldbus or Ethernet, saving long sensor cables. See Chapter 6.3 for how those links stay clean.

figure.caption: One shared 12-bit converter scans 4 of 8 channels at 1 kS/s each, so every conversion has 250 µs and each channel carries signals up to 500 Hz.

spec.title: Elements of a DAS
spec.aria: A left-to-right block chain: transducer, conditioner with 0-5 volt output, an 8-channel multiplexer scanning 4 channels, sample-and-hold, a 12-bit ADC taking 250 microseconds, processor, then store and display.

examples.question: A data acquisition system has 8 input channels and an input range of ±5 V. Its 12-bit ADC is shared by a multiplexer that scans 4 channels, each at 1 kS/s. Find the resolution in volts, the time available for one conversion, and the highest signal frequency each channel can carry.
steps: Full-scale span: V_FS = (+5 V) − (−5 V) = 10 V. The bipolar range spans 10 V, not 5 V.
Resolution: ΔV = V_FS / 2ⁿ = 10 V / 4096 = 2.4414 × 10⁻³ V = 2.44 mV per LSB.
Total converter rate: f_total = 4 channels × 1000 samples/s = 4000 S/s.
Conversion time budget: T_conv = 1 / f_total = 1 / 4000 S/s = 250 × 10⁻⁶ s = 250 µs. Multiplexer settling and sample-and-hold acquisition must fit inside this 250 µs.
Highest signal frequency per channel: f_ch = 1000 S/s, so f_max < f_ch / 2 = 500 Hz.
examples.answer: Resolution is 2.44 mV, each conversion must finish within 250 µs, and each channel carries signals up to 500 Hz.
examples.check:
span = 5 - (-5)          # V, full-scale span for a +/-5 V range
n = 12                   # ADC bits
res = span / 2**n
print(f"resolution = {res * 1000:.4f} mV")

channels = 4             # channels actually scanned
per_channel = 1000       # samples/s on each channel
total = channels * per_channel
print(f"total converter rate = {total} S/s")

t_conv = 1 / total
print(f"conversion time = {t_conv * 1e6:.1f} us")

f_max = per_channel / 2
print(f"max signal frequency = {f_max:.1f} Hz")

traps: Applying the half-sampling-rate rule to the total converter rate instead of the per-channel rate. One shared ADC divides its speed among all scanned channels, so f_max < f_ch / 2, not f_total / 2.

Using 5 V as the span for a ±5 V range. The span is the difference between the limits, 10 V. Using 5 V by mistake gives ΔV half the true value, so the reported resolution is twice as fine as the hardware really is.
Confusing resolution with accuracy. A 12-bit converter has 2.44 mV steps but may be accurate only to 0.1 % of span because of offset, gain and reference errors.

Thinking the sample-and-hold improves resolution. It only holds the value steady. It cuts the smearing from the whole conversion time down to the much shorter aperture time, but it leaves both quantisation error and the residual aperture error unchanged.
Forgetting that acquisition and settling time come out of the same 1/f_total budget, so the ADC's own conversion time must be smaller than that figure.

quiz.q: List the elements of a data acquisition system in signal order, from the physical variable to the stored number.
quiz.a: Transducer → signal conditioner → multiplexer → sample-and-hold → ADC → processor/controller → store and display or bus.

quiz.q: State the formula for the resolution of an n-bit ADC with full-scale span V_FS, defining every symbol.
quiz.a: ΔV = V_FS / 2ⁿ, where ΔV is the resolution in volts (1 LSB), V_FS is the full-scale span in volts and n is the bit count.

quiz.q: Why is a sample-and-hold circuit needed in front of the ADC when the input signal is changing?
quiz.a: The ADC takes a finite time to convert. If the input moves during that time, different bits are decided at different input values, giving an error set by (rate of change) × (conversion or aperture time). The sample-and-hold freezes the voltage on a capacitor so the converter sees one constant value.

quiz.q: A 10-bit ADC has an input range of 0-10 V. Find its resolution in millivolts.
A DAS converter runs at a total of 8000 samples/s and scans 16 channels. Find the per-channel rate and the highest signal frequency each channel can carry.
quiz.a: f_ch = 8000 / 16 = 500 S/s. Then f_max < 500 / 2 = 250 Hz per channel.

quiz.q: What does aperture time mean, and what error does it cause?
quiz.a: Aperture time is the short, uncertain interval during which the sample switch opens. A changing input gives an amplitude error equal to (rate of change of input) × (aperture time).

quiz.q: A student says: with a converter running at 4000 samples/s, every channel can handle signals up to 2 kHz. Identify the mistake and give the correct limit for 4 scanned channels.
quiz.a: The student used the total converter rate instead of the per-channel rate. With 4 channels, f_ch = 4000 / 4 = 1000 S/s, so f_max < 500 Hz per channel.

quiz.q: Compare an 8-bit ADC on a ±5 V range with a 12-bit ADC on a 0-5 V range. Which resolves finer, and what condition must the signal meet?
quiz.a: 8-bit, ±5 V: span 10 V, ΔV = 10 / 256 = 39.1 mV. 12-bit, 0-5 V: ΔV = 5 / 4096 = 1.22 mV. The 12-bit unit resolves about 32 times finer, but the signal must stay inside 0-5 V, so a bipolar signal needs offsetting or it clips.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial DAS has moved toward edge nodes that digitise close to the sensor and publish values over OPC UA or MQTT, so the multiplexer and ADC now sit inside the field device rather than in a central rack. Modern smart sensors often contain their own sigma-delta converter and linearisation table, which shifts the designer's work from wiring to timestamping and data quality. Search for SCADA architecture, programmable automation controller (PAC) input modules, and isolated multi-channel ADC integrated circuits to see the same chain in catalogue form.
